[id="configuring-postgresql-langgraph-agent-state_{context}"]
= Configure PostgreSQL for LangGraph agent state persistence

[role="_abstract"]
You can deploy and configure a PostgreSQL instance on {openshift-platform} to provide persistent storage for LangGraph agent state on {productname-long}.
PostgreSQL serves as the durable backend for Llama Stack agent metadata, response history, and LangGraph graph checkpoints.

.Prerequisites

* You have `cluster-admin` access to the {openshift-platform} cluster.
* A `StorageClass` that supports dynamic provisioning of `PersistentVolumeClaim` resources is available on the cluster.
* You are logged in to the cluster with the {openshift-cli} (`oc`).
* The namespace where the LangGraph agent is deployed exists.

.Procedure

. Create a namespace for the PostgreSQL deployment, or use the same namespace as the agent deployment.
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ oc new-project <postgres_namespace>
----
+
--
Where:

`<postgres_namespace>`:: Specifies the namespace for the PostgreSQL deployment, for example `agent-db`.
--
+
If you use the same namespace as the agent, skip this step.

. Create a Kubernetes `Secret` to store the PostgreSQL credentials.
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ oc create secret generic postgresql-credentials \
  -n <postgres_namespace> \
  --from-literal=POSTGRESQL_USER=<postgres_user> \
  --from-literal=POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD=<postgres_password> \
  --from-literal=POSTGRESQL_DATABASE=<postgres_database>
----
+
--
Where:

`<postgres_user>`:: Specifies the PostgreSQL database user, for example `agent_user`.
`<postgres_password>`:: Specifies a strong password for the database user.
`<postgres_database>`:: Specifies the database name for agent state storage, for example `agent_state`.
--

. Create a `PersistentVolumeClaim` for PostgreSQL data storage.
+
Create a file named `postgresql-pvc.yaml` with the following content:
+
[source,yaml]
----
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: postgresql-data
  namespace: <postgres_namespace>
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
----
+
Apply the `PersistentVolumeClaim`:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ oc apply -f postgresql-pvc.yaml
----
+
[NOTE]
====
The 10Gi storage size is suitable for development and testing workloads.
For production deployments with high volumes of agent conversations or large state objects, increase the storage size based on your expected data growth.
====

. Deploy PostgreSQL on {openshift-platform}.
+
Create a file named `postgresql-deployment.yaml` with the following content:
+
[source,yaml]
----
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: postgresql
  namespace: <postgres_namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgresql
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: postgresql
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgresql
        image: registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
        env:
        - name: POSTGRESQL_USER
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: postgresql-credentials
              key: POSTGRESQL_USER
        - name: POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: postgresql-credentials
              key: POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD
        - name: POSTGRESQL_DATABASE
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: postgresql-credentials
              key: POSTGRESQL_DATABASE
        readinessProbe:
          exec:
            command:
              - /usr/libexec/check-container
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          exec:
            command:
              - /usr/libexec/check-container
              - --live
          initialDelaySeconds: 120
          periodSeconds: 10
        volumeMounts:
        - name: postgresql-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/pgsql/data
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 250m
            memory: 512Mi
          limits:
            cpu: "1"
            memory: 1Gi
      volumes:
      - name: postgresql-data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: postgresql-data
----
+
The `initialDelaySeconds` value of `120` allows time for PostgreSQL to complete first-time database initialization, including creating the data directory and system catalogs.
+
Apply the deployment:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ oc apply -f postgresql-deployment.yaml
----

. Create a `Service` to expose PostgreSQL within the cluster.
+
Create a file named `postgresql-service.yaml` with the following content:
+
[source,yaml]
----
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: postgresql
  namespace: <postgres_namespace>
spec:
  selector:
    app: postgresql
  ports:
  - port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
  type: ClusterIP
----
+
Apply the service:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ oc apply -f postgresql-service.yaml
----

. Wait for the PostgreSQL pod to reach `Running` status.
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ oc get pods -n <postgres_namespace> -l app=postgresql -w
----
+
Wait until the `STATUS` column shows `Running` and the `READY` column shows `1/1`.

[id="deploying-langgraph-agent-to-rhoai_{context}"]
= Deploy a LangGraph agent from local development to {productname-short}

[role="_abstract"]
You can deploy a LangGraph agent that you developed and tested locally to {productname-long} by reconfiguring provider settings, building a container image, and deploying with the shared Helm chart.
To complete the deployment, you verify the local agent, configure production providers, build and push a container image, and deploy to OpenShift with Helm.

[NOTE]
====
MLflow-based observability and tracing integration for LangGraph agents is planned for a future release.
This procedure does not include MLflow configuration steps.
====

.Prerequisites

* You have access to a {productname-long} {vernum} cluster.
* The Llama Stack operator is installed on the cluster.
* Model serving is configured with vLLM or llm-d through a KServe `InferenceService`.
* A vector storage service, such as Milvus or PGVector, is available and accessible from the cluster.
* You are logged in to the cluster with the {openshift-cli} (`oc`).
* The Helm CLI is installed on your local machine.
* You have access to a container image registry that the cluster can pull images from.
* Python 3.12 or later is installed on your local machine.
* The `uv` package manager is installed on your local machine. See link:https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/[uv installation documentation].
* The `openai` Python SDK version 1.109.1 or later is installed (`openai>=1.109.1`). This version is required for `McpCall` response parsing when using Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools.
* You have a locally-developed and tested LangGraph agent application. For example agent templates, see the link:https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits[agentic starter kits repository].

.Procedure

. Verify that your agent runs locally with local providers.
+
Start the Llama Stack server with your local `run.yaml` configuration and confirm that the agent responds correctly:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ uv run llama stack run run.yaml --image-type venv
----
+
In a separate terminal, start your agent application and submit a test request:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ python app.py
----

. Configure the provider swap by updating the `.env` file with production values.
+
Create or update the `.env` file in your agent project directory with the following production settings:
+
[source,terminal]
----
# Inference provider configuration
LLAMA_STACK_SERVER_OPENAI=http://<llama_stack_route>/v1/openai/v1
INFERENCE_MODEL=<provider_id>/<model_id>
OPENAI_API_KEY=<api_key>
VLLM_INFERENCE_URL=<vllm_inference_url>

# MCP tool configuration (if applicable)
MCP_TOOL_MODEL=<provider_id>/<model_id>
GIT_TOKEN=<github_personal_access_token>
GITHUB_URL=https://github.com/<organization>/<repository>
GITHUB_ID=<github_user_id>
----
+
--
Where:

`<vllm_inference_url>`:: Specifies the URL of the vLLM inference endpoint. For in-cluster access, use the KServe `InferenceService` URL, for example `http://vllm-service.my-namespace.svc.cluster.local:8000/v1`. For external access, use the OpenShift Route URL.
`<llama_stack_route>`:: Specifies the hostname of the Llama Stack server running on {productname-short}. Do not include the `/v1/openai/v1` path -- it is already appended in the variable value. For in-cluster access, use the Kubernetes service URL, for example `llama-stack-server.my-namespace.svc.cluster.local:8321`. For access through an OpenShift Route, use the route hostname, for example `llama-stack-my-namespace.apps.cluster.example.com`.
`<provider_id>/<model_id>`:: Specifies the model name as registered in Llama Stack, for example `vllm/qwen3-8b-fp8`. The `vllm/` or `ollama/` prefix is a Llama Stack model registration convention. In `app.py`, `init_chat_model` always uses `model_provider="openai"` because all inference goes through Llama Stack's OpenAI-compatible API.
`<api_key>`:: Specifies the API key for the model serving endpoint.
`<github_personal_access_token>`:: Specifies a GitHub personal access token with permission to create issues. Required only if the agent uses the GitHub MCP Server.
--
+
[NOTE]
====
The `LLAMA_STACK_SERVER_OPENAI` URL includes the path `/v1/openai/v1` because the Llama Stack server exposes its OpenAI-compatible endpoint at this path relative to its base URL.
Both `/v1` segments are required: the first is the Llama Stack API version prefix, and the second is the OpenAI API version prefix.
====

. Update the Llama Stack `run.yaml` provider configuration to point at production services.
+
Modify the `providers.inference` section to use the vLLM provider instead of Ollama:
+
[source,yaml]
----
providers:
  inference:
  - provider_id: vllm
    provider_type: remote::vllm
    config:
      url: ${env.VLLM_INFERENCE_URL}
      api_token: ${env.OPENAI_API_KEY}
      max_tokens: 4096
      tls_verify: false
----
+
If your agent uses vector storage, update the `providers.vector_io` section to point at your production Milvus or PGVector instance.
If your agent uses persistent state, update the `providers.agents` section to use PostgreSQL instead of SQLite.

. Build the container image using the provided Dockerfile and push it to your registry.
+
The agentic starter kits provide a Dockerfile based on UBI9 with Python 3.12.
+
[IMPORTANT]
====
The reference agent application (`app.py`) runs Flask with `debug=True`.
You must replace the entrypoint with a production Web Server Gateway Interface (WSGI) server before building the production container image.
Running Flask with `debug=True` in production exposes the interactive debugger, which allows arbitrary code execution.

In `app.py`, change `debug=True` to `debug=False`.
Then update the `CMD` instruction in your Dockerfile to use `gunicorn`:

[source,docker]
----
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8080", "app:app"]
----

Add `gunicorn` to your project dependencies:

[source,terminal]
----
$ uv add gunicorn
----
====
+
Build the image:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ podman build -t <registry>/<namespace>/<image_name>:<tag> .
----
+
Push the image to your registry:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ podman push <registry>/<namespace>/<image_name>:<tag>
----
+
--
Where:

`<registry>`:: Specifies the container image registry URL.
`<namespace>`:: Specifies the registry namespace or project.
`<image_name>`:: Specifies the name for your agent container image.
`<tag>`:: Specifies the image tag, for example `latest` or `v1.0`.
--

. Configure the Helm values for your specific agent variant.
+
The agentic starter kits provide a shared Helm chart at `charts/agent/` with per-agent value override files.
Copy the values override file for your agent variant and update it with your production settings:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ cp agents/langgraph/<agent_variant>/values.yaml my-values.yaml
----
+
Edit `my-values.yaml` to set your container image, environment variables, and resource requirements:
+
[source,yaml]
----
image:
  repository: <registry>/<namespace>/<image_name>
  tag: <tag>
env:
  INFERENCE_MODEL: "<provider_id>/<model_id>"
  LLAMA_STACK_SERVER_OPENAI: "http://<llama_stack_route>/v1/openai/v1"
----
+
--
Where:

`<agent_variant>`:: Specifies the agent template directory name: `react_agent`, `agentic_rag`, or `react_with_database_memory`.
--

. Deploy the agent to OpenShift by using the Helm chart.
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ helm install <release_name> charts/agent/ -f my-values.yaml -n <namespace>
----
+
--
Where:

`<release_name>`:: Specifies a unique name for the Helm release, for example `my-react-agent`.
`<namespace>`:: Specifies the OpenShift project where the agent is deployed.
--
+
Alternatively, if the agent variant provides Make targets, you can use them:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ cd agents/langgraph/<agent_variant> && make deploy
----

[id="local-to-production-provider-swap-architecture_{context}"]
= Local-to-production provider swap architecture for LangGraph agents

[role="_abstract"]
You can deploy a LangGraph agent that you built and tested on your local machine to {productname-long} by changing provider configuration for inference, vector storage, and state providers, without modifying your application code.
The Llama Stack API serves as a standardized provider abstraction layer between your agent application and infrastructure services, routing requests to the appropriate backend provider based on configuration.

The agentic starter kits offer production-ready agent templates that use the Llama Stack API as a common interface.
By updating environment variables and Llama Stack configuration files, you swap local development providers for production services running on {productname-short}.
Your application code interacts only with the Llama Stack OpenAI-compatible API, so the same code runs unchanged in both environments.

== Provider abstraction layer

The Llama Stack API acts as a proxy between your LangGraph agent and the underlying infrastructure services.
In local development, you configure Llama Stack to route requests to lightweight providers such as Ollama for inference and Chroma for vector storage.
In production on {productname-short}, you reconfigure Llama Stack to route the same requests to enterprise-grade services such as vLLM or llm-d for inference and Milvus or PGVector for vector storage.

Because the API contract between your agent and Llama Stack remains the same, your application code does not change for inference, vector storage, and state providers.
Only the Llama Stack configuration and environment variables differ between environments.
Tool integration might require code changes to define Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool objects and pass them to the Responses API.
For more information about MCP tool integration, see xref:mcp-tool-integration-llama-stack_{context}[MCP tool integration with the Llama Stack tools API].

The following table shows how each agentic component maps from local development providers to production providers on {productname-short}.

.Provider mapping for local and production environments
[cols="1,1,1,1", options="header"]
|===
|Component
|Local provider
|Production provider
|Key environment variables

|Inference
|Ollama
|vLLM or llm-d via KServe InferenceService
|`INFERENCE_MODEL`, `LLAMA_STACK_SERVER_OPENAI`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`

|Vector storage
|Chroma or Milvus Lite
|Milvus or PGVector
|`MILVUS_URL`, `MILVUS_DB_PATH`

|State and memory
|SQLite or in-memory
|PostgreSQL. See xref:maintaining-agent-state-in-production[Maintain agent state and reliability in production].
|Configured in `run.yaml` under `providers.agents`

|Tools
|Local functions
|MCP servers: Kubernetes MCP Server, GitHub MCP Server
|`MCP_TOOL_MODEL`, `GIT_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_URL`

|Observability
|Local MLflow
|{productname-short} MLflow (planned -- not available in {vernum})
|`MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI`, `MLFLOW_EXPERIMENT_NAME` -- do not configure in {vernum}
|===

[NOTE]
====
MLflow-based observability and tracing for agentic applications is planned for a future release of {productname-short}.
Do not configure MLflow tracing environment variables for agent deployments in {productname-long} {vernum}.
====

== Configuration layers

The local-to-production migration involves four configuration layers.
Each layer controls a different aspect of the deployment.

`.env` file:: Specifies environment variables for inference endpoints, model identifiers, API keys, and MCP tool configuration. This file is the primary mechanism for switching between local and production providers.

`run.yaml`:: Defines the Llama Stack provider configuration. Each section, including `providers.inference`, `providers.vector_io`, `providers.agents`, `providers.tool_runtime`, and `providers.safety`, specifies which backend provider to use and how to connect to it. Environment variable substitution within `run.yaml` allows the same file to adapt to both environments.

Helm `values.yaml`:: Controls the Kubernetes deployment configuration, including the container image, resource limits, environment variable injection, and OpenShift route configuration. Per-agent value overrides customize the deployment for each agent variant.

Agent-specific configuration:: Defines agent behavior, including the LangGraph workflow, structured output schemas, and tool definitions. This configuration is part of your application code and does not change between environments.

== {productname-short}-managed and user-managed components

When deploying LangGraph agents on {productname-short}, some infrastructure components are managed by {productname-short} and some must be managed by the cluster administrator or the developer.

{productname-short}-managed components::
* Llama Stack operator and `LlamaStackDistribution` custom resource
* Model serving via KServe `InferenceService` with vLLM or llm-d runtime
* MLflow operator and tracking server (when enabled)

User-managed components::
* Vector storage services such as Milvus or PGVector
* PostgreSQL for agent state persistence
* MCP server deployments such as Kubernetes MCP Server and GitHub MCP Server
* Container image builds and registry management

[IMPORTANT]
====
The Helm chart provided by the agentic starter kits generates only `Deployment`, `Service`, `Route`, and `Secret` resources for your agent application.
The Llama Stack operator, `InferenceService`, and vector storage services are cluster prerequisites that must be configured separately before deploying your agent.
====

== Available agent templates

The agentic starter kits include the following LangGraph agent variants:

ReAct Agent:: A general-purpose agent that uses the ReAct pattern for reasoning and acting. Supports tool calling through MCP servers.

Agentic RAG:: An agent that combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with agentic reasoning. Connects to vector storage for document retrieval.

ReAct with Database Memory:: A ReAct agent with persistent state backed by PostgreSQL. Maintains conversation history across sessions.

Human-in-the-Loop:: An agent that includes approval checkpoints for human review before executing certain actions.

Each variant uses the same Llama Stack provider abstraction and can be deployed using the shared Helm chart with per-agent value overrides.

[NOTE]
====
The agentic starter kits also include a LlamaIndex WebSearch Agent.
For information about LlamaIndex agents, see the link:https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits/tree/main/agents[agentic starter kits repository].
====

[role="_additional-resources"]
.Additional resources

* link:https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits[Agentic starter kits repository]
* link:https://llamastack.readthedocs.io/[Llama Stack documentation]
* link:https://github.com/opendatahub-io/agents/tree/main/examples/langchain-langgraph[LangChain and LangGraph reference agent implementation]

ifdef::context[:parent-context: {context}]

[id="maintaining-agent-state-in-production"]
= Maintain agent state and reliability in production

:context: maintaining-agent-state

[role="_abstract"]
You can configure persistent state backends for LangGraph agents on {productname-long} to ensure that conversation history, agent checkpoints, and accumulated context survive pod restarts, scaling events, and cluster maintenance.
By default, LangGraph agents use in-memory or file-based storage that is lost when a pod is rescheduled.
Transitioning to PostgreSQL provides production-grade durability for agent state.

To maintain agent state in production, you must understand the two-layer state model, choose the appropriate storage backend, provision PostgreSQL, and configure both the Llama Stack metadata store and the LangGraph checkpointer.

.Prerequisites

* A LangGraph agent is deployed to {productname-short}. See xref:deploying-langgraph-agents-from-local-to-rhoai[Deploy LangGraph agents from local development to {productname-short}].
* You have `cluster-admin` access or a namespace administrator can provision PostgreSQL resources.
* A `StorageClass` that supports dynamic provisioning of `PersistentVolumeClaim` resources is available on the cluster.

# Documentation Plan

**Project**: Bring your agent built on your laptop with LangGraph to RH AI
**Date**: 2026-06-11
**Ticket**: [RHAISTRAT-1393](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393)

## What is the support status of the feature(s) being used to complete the user's JTBD (Job To Be Done)?

Technology Preview. Llama Stack is Technology Preview in RHOAI 3.4. The MCP catalog is Developer Preview. The MCP gateway is Technology Preview. The Tool Runtime API (/v1/tool-runtime) is Developer Preview. All documentation must include the appropriate Technology Preview or Developer Preview disclaimers.

## Why is this content important?

Developers building AI agents with LangChain/LangGraph face a painful gap between local prototyping and production deployment on Red Hat OpenShift AI. Today they must reverse-engineer provider configurations, manually create Kubernetes manifests, re-engineer state management, and figure out tool integration patterns from scattered upstream sources. This documentation eliminates that friction by providing a single, end-to-end path from a locally running LangGraph agent to a production RHOAI deployment, using only configuration changes. Without it, what should be a repeatable deployment procedure becomes a multi-week integration effort, increasing time to value and eroding confidence in the RHOAI platform.

## Who is the target persona(s)?

* Developer: Primary user building LangChain/LangGraph-based AI agents locally and deploying them to RHOAI. Needs step-by-step guidance for the local-to-production journey, provider configuration, and MCP tool integration.
* SysAdmin: Manages the OpenShift cluster and RHOAI platform where agents are deployed. Responsible for infrastructure prerequisites (GPU nodes, Llama Stack Operator, KServe, persistent storage, MCP server deployment) and needs reference documentation for Kubernetes manifests and cluster configuration.

## What is the main JTBD? What user goal is being accomplished? What pain point is being avoided?

**Developer job**: When I have built and tested a LangGraph agent locally using Ollama and in-memory state, I want to deploy that same agent to Red Hat OpenShift AI by changing only provider configuration, so that I can run my agent in production with enterprise-grade inference, persistent storage, and managed tools while avoiding code refactoring, re-engineering state management, and manual infrastructure configuration.

**SysAdmin job**: When the development team needs to run LangGraph agents in production on our OpenShift cluster, I want to provision and configure the required infrastructure (model serving, persistent storage, MCP servers, observability) using documented Kubernetes manifests and operator CRDs, so that I can provide a reliable platform for agent workloads while avoiding misconfigured deployments and undocumented dependencies.

## How does the JTBD(s) relate to the overall real-world workflow for the user?

This documentation sits at the center of the "Zero to Production" developer journey for agentic AI on Red Hat OpenShift AI (the parent outcome defined in RHAISTRAT-1049). The workflow spans five phases:

1. **Local development** (Developer): Clone the agentic-starter-kits repository, install UV and dependencies, configure a local Llama Stack server with Ollama, and run a LangGraph agent variant (ReAct, Agentic RAG, database memory, human-in-the-loop) against local providers.
2. **Provider configuration** (Developer + SysAdmin): Map each capability layer (inference, vector storage, memory/state, tools) from local providers to their RHOAI production equivalents using the Llama Stack provider abstraction. The SysAdmin ensures the target infrastructure (vLLM via KServe, Milvus/PGVector, PostgreSQL/Redis, MCP servers) is provisioned.
3. **Deployment** (SysAdmin + Developer): Apply Kubernetes manifests or Helm charts to deploy the agent container, Llama Stack server, and supporting services to OpenShift. The Developer verifies the agent REST API endpoint; the SysAdmin monitors cluster resource usage.
4. **Observability** (Developer): Enable MLflow tracing to capture agent execution flows, LLM call spans, tool invocations, and token usage for debugging and evaluation (targeting RHOAI 3.5 per RHAISTRAT-1364 deferral).
5. **Day-2 operations** (SysAdmin): Manage persistent state backends, scale agent deployments, register and govern MCP tool servers through the catalog and gateway, and troubleshoot production issues.

The documentation also feeds into the broader RHOAI Llama Stack guide (Working with Llama Stack), extending the existing server deployment content with application-level agent deployment.

## What high-level steps does the user need to take to accomplish the goal?

**Prerequisites**:
- OpenShift 4.19+ cluster with GPU nodes
- RHOAI 3.4 installed with Llama Stack Operator activated
- KServe / OpenShift Serverless installed
- Python 3.12 and UV package manager installed locally
- Container image registry access

**Developer steps**:
1. Clone the agentic-starter-kits repository and set up local development environment
2. Configure the local Llama Stack server (run_llama_server.yaml) with Ollama
3. Run a LangGraph agent variant locally and verify it works
4. Modify provider configuration to target RHOAI components (vLLM, Milvus, PostgreSQL, MCP servers)
5. Build the agent container image and push to registry
6. Deploy to OpenShift using the shared Helm chart (charts/agent/)
7. Verify the deployed agent REST API endpoint
8. (Optional) Enable MLflow tracing for observability

**SysAdmin steps**:
1. Deploy a KServe InferenceService for vLLM model serving
2. Create a LlamaStackDistribution CR with production provider configuration
3. Provision persistent storage (PostgreSQL, PVC for embeddings/checkpoints)
4. Deploy and register MCP tool servers
5. Create Service and Route resources for external API access
6. Verify pod readiness and endpoint health

## Is there a demo available or can one be created?

Yes. The agentic-starter-kits repository at https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits contains working LangGraph agent examples (react_agent, agentic_rag, react_with_database_memory, human_in_the_loop) with local and OpenShift deployment instructions.

## Are there special considerations for disconnected environments?

Yes. Disconnected (air-gapped) environments require:
- Pre-pulling the Llama Stack operator image and agent container images into a local registry
- Local mirror of the model weights served by vLLM
- MCP servers must be deployed within the cluster rather than accessing external SSE endpoints
- The Helm chart values must be configured to point to internal registry and service URLs

## Who can provide information and answer questions?

- **PM**: Participant B (moved ticket to Release Pending, strategic owner of RHAISTRAT-1393)
- **Technical SME**: Participant A (implementation lead, confirmed feature completion), Participant D (WIP implementation at MRGuziX/Agentic-Starter-Kits, vLLM via KServe work), Participant F (confirmed AC points 1-2 completed in agentic-starter-kits)
- **MLflow tracing SME**: Participant C (emphasized MLflow tracing importance for agentic evaluation, scope split to RHAISTRAT-1364)
- **Release note assignee**: Kelly Brown (RHAIENG-4404)

## Release Note needed?

Yes.

Draft release note: Red Hat OpenShift AI 3.4 introduces agentic starter kits that enable you to build and deploy AI agents using LangGraph (LangChain) and LlamaIndex frameworks. The starter kits, hosted in the [agentic-starter-kits repository](https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits/tree/main/agents), provide production-ready agent templates including ReAct, Agentic RAG, ReAct with database memory, and human-in-the-loop agents for LangGraph, and a web search agent for LlamaIndex. You can develop agents locally using Ollama and deploy them to OpenShift AI through configuration changes alone, using Llama Stack as the standardized provider layer. Llama Stack is a Technology Preview feature.

## Links to existing content

* [RHOAI 3.4 Working with Llama Stack - Deploying Llama Stack server](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_ai_self-managed/3.4/html/working_with_llama_stack/deploying-llama-stack-server_rag) -- Existing prerequisite: deploying the Llama Stack server that agents connect to
* [RHOAI 3.4 Release Notes - New features](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_ai_self-managed/3.4/html/release_notes/new-features-and-enhancements_relnotes) -- Target location for the release note entry
* [RHOAI 3.2 Llama Stack Application Examples](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_ai_self-managed/3.2/html/working_with_llama_stack/llama-stack-adv-examples_rag) -- Previous version application examples for structural reference
* [OpenDataHub Llama Stack docs](https://opendatahub.io/docs/working-with-llama-stack/) -- Upstream community docs for run.yaml schema and provider types
* [agentic-starter-kits repository](https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits) -- Source code and reference implementation for all agent templates
* [LangGraph Persistence Documentation](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/persistence) -- Upstream LangGraph checkpointer/persistence docs
* [LangChain MCP adapters](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/mcp) -- Upstream MCP integration library docs

---

## Documentation impact assessment

| Requirement | Impact | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| REQ-001: LangGraph agent local-to-RHOAI tutorial | **High** | Major new end-to-end tutorial for a flagship RHOAI 3.4 feature; completely new user workflow |
| REQ-002: Provider configuration swap reference | **High** | New reference documentation for the core abstraction that enables the feature; no existing equivalent |
| REQ-003: Kubernetes deployment manifests | **High** | New deployment artifacts documentation; users cannot deploy without this reference |
| REQ-004: Agent state persistence | **High** | New capability area; state loss in production is a critical failure mode |
| REQ-005: MLflow observability and tracing | **Medium** | Important but deferred to RHOAI 3.5 (RHAISTRAT-1364 fix_version rhoai-3.5.EA1); plan now, publish later |
| REQ-006: Release note | **High** | Required for GA release; consolidated entry covering both LangGraph and LlamaIndex |
| REQ-007: MCP tool integration | **Medium** | New capability with multiple support levels (Dev Preview, Tech Preview); important but complex and partially preview-status |

## Relationship analysis

| Pair | Relationship | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| REQ-001 / REQ-002 | **Complementary** | The tutorial (REQ-001) references the provider mapping reference (REQ-002) as its configuration backbone |
| REQ-001 / REQ-003 | **Overlapping** | Both describe deploying to OpenShift; REQ-001 takes the Helm chart path while REQ-003 covers raw manifests. Consolidation needed: the tutorial should use Helm and link to the manifest reference for users who need lower-level control |
| REQ-001 / REQ-004 | **Sequential** | REQ-004 (state persistence) is a configuration step within the REQ-001 deployment workflow |
| REQ-001 / REQ-005 | **Sequential** | REQ-005 (MLflow) adds an observability layer after deployment; deferred to 3.5 |
| REQ-002 / REQ-003 | **Complementary** | REQ-002 provides the configuration reference; REQ-003 provides the manifest reference. Different module types covering different aspects |
| REQ-002 / REQ-004 | **Complementary** | REQ-004 covers the memory provider row in REQ-002's mapping table in depth |
| REQ-002 / REQ-007 | **Complementary** | REQ-007 covers the tools provider row in REQ-002's mapping table in depth |
| REQ-003 / REQ-004 | **Complementary** | REQ-004 adds PVC and database prerequisites to the manifests in REQ-003 |
| REQ-006 / all others | **Independent** | Release note is a standalone artifact referencing the feature but structurally separate |

## Theme clusters

### Cluster 1: Core tutorial and deployment journey
- **Summary**: End-to-end developer journey from local LangGraph agent to production on RHOAI
- **Issues included**: REQ-001, REQ-003, portions of REQ-002 (concept), portions of REQ-004 (deployment steps)
- **Overlap risk**: High (REQ-001 and REQ-003 both cover OpenShift deployment)
- **Recommended ownership**: Assembly "Deploy LangGraph agents from local development to production" under the Deploy category
- **Resolution**: REQ-001 tutorial uses the Helm chart as the primary path. REQ-003 provides the manifest-level reference for users who need to understand or customize individual resources. The tutorial links to the manifest reference rather than duplicating YAML examples.

### Cluster 2: Provider configuration and architecture reference
- **Summary**: Llama Stack provider abstraction, mapping tables, and run.yaml parameter reference
- **Issues included**: REQ-002, the reference module from REQ-001
- **Overlap risk**: Medium (REQ-001's provider configuration reference overlaps with REQ-002's mapping table)
- **Recommended ownership**: Assembly "Configure Llama Stack providers for local and production environments" under the Configure category
- **Resolution**: Consolidate into REQ-002's modules. REQ-001's `ref-langgraph-agent-provider-configuration.adoc` is merged into REQ-002's `ref-llama-stack-provider-mapping.adoc` to avoid two overlapping provider tables.

### Cluster 3: Production hardening (state and observability)
- **Summary**: Persistent state backends and MLflow tracing for production agent reliability
- **Issues included**: REQ-004, REQ-005
- **Overlap risk**: Low
- **Recommended ownership**: Assembly "Operate LangGraph agents in production" under the Operate category. REQ-005 (MLflow) deferred to RHOAI 3.5 planning.

### Cluster 4: MCP tool integration
- **Summary**: MCP server registration, local-to-production tool transitions, and the MCP catalog
- **Issues included**: REQ-007
- **Overlap risk**: Low (self-contained; links to Cluster 2 for provider mapping tools row)
- **Recommended ownership**: Assembly "Extend agent capabilities with MCP tools" under the Extend category

### Cluster 5: Release note
- **Summary**: Consolidated release note for agentic starter kits
- **Issues included**: REQ-006
- **Overlap risk**: None
- **Recommended ownership**: RHOAI 3.4 release notes guide, New features and enhancements chapter

  "summary": "Red Hat OpenShift AI 3.4 introduces agentic starter kits that allow developers to build LangChain/LangGraph agents locally (using Ollama, in-memory vector stores, file-based state) and deploy them to RHOAI through configuration changes alone, without modifying application code. {
  "id": "REQ-004",
  "title": "Agent state persistence in production",
  "priority": "high",
  "category": "new_feature",
  "sources": [
    {"label": "RHAISTRAT-1393", "url": "https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393", "note": "Main feature ticket defining local-to-production agent deployment including state persistence via Llama Stack memory API"},
    {"label": "RHAIRFE-1172", "url": "https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172", "note": "Feature request specifying acceptance criterion: agent state and memory must persist across pod restarts in production"}
  ],
  "summary": "LangGraph agents developed locally use ephemeral in-memory or file-based state (MemorySaver, SQLite) that is lost on process restart. When deploying to Red Hat OpenShift AI, agent state and memory must transition to durable, production-grade persistent storage — PostgreSQL (via the Llama Stack memory API and the LlamaStackDistribution CR) or Redis (via LangGraph's RedisSaver checkpointer). This documentation requirement covers the configuration-driven swap from local ephemeral storage to persistent backends, the Llama Stack memory provider abstraction that makes this transparent to application code, and the PersistentVolumeClaim and database prerequisites needed on OpenShift.",
  "user_impact": "Without this documentation, developers deploying LangGraph agents to RHOAI will lose agent conversation history, RAG context, and checkpoint state on every pod restart or scaling event, resulting in broken multi-turn conversations and failed agentic workflows. Users need clear guidance on configuring persistent backends so their agents maintain state continuity in production without code changes.",
  "scope": "new",
  "documentation_actions": [
    {"action": "Create", "file": "con-agent-state-persistence-overview.adoc", "type": "CONCEPT", "note": "Explain the two-layer memory model (short-term checkpoints vs long-term memory), local-vs-production storage backends, and how the Llama Stack memory API abstracts the provider swap"},
    {"action": "Create", "file": "proc-configuring-persistent-state-for-langgraph-agents.adoc", "type": "PROCEDURE", "note": "Step-by-step procedure for transitioning from local MemorySaver/SQLite to PostgreSQL or Redis checkpointers when deploying to RHOAI, including LlamaStackDistribution CR memory provider configuration"},
    {"action": "Create", "file": "ref-agent-state-storage-backends.adoc", "type": "REFERENCE", "note": "Reference table comparing storage backends (in-memory, SQLite, PostgreSQL, Redis) with latency characteristics, durability guarantees, scaling properties, and recommended use cases"},
    {"action": "Create", "file": "proc-configuring-postgresql-for-agent-state.adoc", "type": "PROCEDURE", "note": "Procedure for setting up PostgreSQL as the persistent backend for Llama Stack metadata and agent state, including prerequisites (PostgreSQL 14+, credentials, network access), environment variables (POSTGRES_HOST, POSTGRES_PORT), and PVC configuration"},
    {"action": "Update", "file": "proc-deploying-langgraph-agent-to-rhoai.adoc", "type": "PROCEDURE", "note": "Add state persistence configuration section to the main deployment procedure, cross-referencing the detailed persistence procedures and ensuring the Deployment manifest includes LLAMA_STACK_BASE_URL and checkpointer configuration"}
  ],
  "acceptance_criteria": [
    "Users can identify which local storage backend (MemorySaver, SQLite, file-based) their LangGraph agent uses and its production-equivalent persistent backend",

    "Users can configure Redis as an alternative checkpointing backend for LangGraph agents by following the documented procedure",

  ],

    {"label": "RHAIRFE-1172 AC-2", "url": "https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172", "note": "Acceptance criterion: Agent state and memory persist across pod restarts in production environment"},
    {"label": "RHAIRFE-1172 Comment (Participant F)", "url": "https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172", "note": "Confirmation that basic repo and README for state persistence (points 1 and 2) are completed in agentic-starter-kits repo"},
    {"label": "RHAISTRAT-1393 Provider Table", "url": "https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393", "note": "Memory row: Local file system / SQLite -> PV - postgres etc. (enabled via the llama-stack memory API)"},

    {"label": "Agentic Starter Kits - LangGraph React Agent", "url": "https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits/tree/main/agents/base/langgraph_react_agent", "note": "Completed starter kit with state persistence implementation referenced in RHAIRFE-1172 comments"}
  ],
  "web_findings": [
    {"title": "Build smarter AI agents with LangGraph and Redis", "url": "https://redis.io/blog/langgraph-redis-build-smarter-ai-agents-with-memory-persistence/", "relevance": "Comprehensive guide to LangGraph + Redis checkpointing integration using RedisSaver, including production deployment patterns and fault-tolerance"},
    {"title": "LangGraph Redis Checkpoint 0.1.0", "url": "https://redis.io/blog/langgraph-redis-checkpoint-010/", "relevance": "Latest Redis checkpoint architecture with denormalized storage and sub-millisecond retrieval for production AI agent state"},

    {"title": "Working with Llama Stack - Open Data Hub", "url": "https://opendatahub.io/docs/working-with-llama-stack/", "relevance": "Open Data Hub documentation for LlamaStackDistribution CR configuration including memory/persistence providers and PostgreSQL as default metadata store"},
    {"title": "Red Hat OpenShift AI Llama Stack Application Examples", "url": "https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_ai_self-managed/3.2/html/working_with_llama_stack/llama-stack-adv-examples_rag", "relevance": "Official Red Hat documentation showing Llama Stack configuration for RAG and agentic applications on RHOAI 3.2"},
    {"title": "Agent State Management: Redis vs Postgres for AI Memory", "url": "https://www.sitepoint.com/state-management-for-long-running-agents-redis-vs-postgres/", "relevance": "Comparison of Redis vs PostgreSQL for agent state with durability trade-offs, latency benchmarks, and hybrid architecture recommendations"},
    {"title": "Deploying agents with Red Hat AI: The curious case of OpenClaw", "url": "https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2026/04/14/deploying-agents-red-hat-ai-openclaw", "relevance": "Practical example of agent state management on RHOAI including SQLite persistence considerations and OpenShift security constraints"},
    {"title": "Automate AI agents with the Responses API in Llama Stack", "url": "https://developers.redhat.com/articles/2026/03/09/automate-ai-agents-responses-api-llama-stack", "relevance": "Red Hat Developer article showing PostgreSQL Saver integration with LangGraph state via the Llama Stack Responses API"}
  ],
  "is_breaking_change": false,
  "deprecation_version": null,
  "notes": "PostgreSQL is the default and recommended metadata store for Llama Stack on RHOAI starting with version 3.2, replacing SQLite for production. The agentic-starter-kits repo (red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits) reportedly has the basic state persistence implementation completed per RHAIRFE-1172 comments (Participant F, 2026-02-26), but no repository access was verified. The Llama Stack memory API provides the abstraction layer that enables configuration-only provider swaps, but documentation must also cover LangGraph-native checkpointers (RedisSaver, PostgresSaver) for cases where agents use LangGraph's built-in persistence directly rather than going through the Llama Stack memory API. The RHAISTRAT-1393 ticket is in 'Release Pending' status, indicating the feature implementation is complete for RHOAI 3.4."
}

  ],
  "is_breaking_change": false,
  "deprecation_version": null,
  "notes": "RHAISTRAT-1364 was deferred from RHOAI 3.4 documentation scope (docs team capacity constraints per comment from 2026-04-09) but the feature was later confirmed by PM and moved to Release Pending with fix_version rhoai-3.5.EA1. The parent ticket RHAISTRAT-1393 (rhoai-3.4) references MLflow as acceptance criterion #3 but delegates to RHAISTRAT-1364. Documentation for this requirement may need to target RHOAI 3.5 rather than 3.4. The agentic-starter-kits repo does not yet contain MLflow tracing code — the Langflow agent uses Langfuse v3 instead — confirming this is net-new work. MLflow tracing for LangGraph is an extension of the LangChain integration via mlflow.langchain.autolog(); only trace logging is supported for LangGraph (not full model autologging). MLflow 3+ is recommended for best tracing experience."

The release note author should confirm with the RHAIENG-4404 assignee whether the scope has expanded beyond the original two frameworks or remains limited to LangGraph and LlamaIndex as specified in the ticket description."
}

# Documentation Requirements

**Source**: Bring your agent built on your laptop with LangGraph to RH AI
**Date**: 2026-06-11
**Release/Sprint**: rhoai-3.4

## Summary

- Total requirements analyzed: 7
- New modules needed: 24
- Existing modules to update: 5
- Breaking changes requiring docs: 0

## Requirements by priority

### Critical

#### REQ-001: LangChain/LangGraph agent local-to-RHOAI deployment tutorial
- **Source**: [RHAISTRAT-1393](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393) | [RHAIRFE-1172](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172) | [RHAISTRAT-1049 (parent)](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1049) | [RHAIENG-4404 (linked)](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIENG-4404)
- **Summary**: Red Hat OpenShift AI 3.4 introduces agentic starter kits that allow developers to build LangChain/LangGraph agents locally (using Ollama, in-memory vector stores, file-based state) and deploy them to RHOAI through configuration changes alone, without modifying application code. The Llama Stack API serves as the standardized provider layer that abstracts the underlying infrastructure, enabling a configuration-driven swap from local providers to enterprise-grade RHOAI components (vLLM/llm-d for inference, Milvus/PGVector for vector storage, PostgreSQL/Redis for state persistence, MCP servers for tools). A comprehensive tutorial is needed to guide developers through this end-to-end journey, covering local setup with the agentic-starter-kits repository, provider configuration mapping, Helm-based deployment to OpenShift, and verification of the running agent via its REST API endpoint.
- **User impact**: Developers building agentic AI applications with LangChain and LangGraph currently face significant friction when moving from local development to production on RHOAI, requiring code refactoring to swap providers, re-engineering state management, and manual infrastructure configuration. This tutorial eliminates that friction by documenting the configuration-only deployment path, reducing a multi-week integration effort to a repeatable procedure that preserves the same agent code across environments.
- **Documentation action**:
  - [ ] Create `con-langgraph-agent-local-to-production-overview.adoc` (CONCEPT) Explain the local-to-production architecture: how Llama Stack abstracts providers, the configuration-driven swap pattern, and why no code changes are needed. Include the provider mapping table (Inference, Vector DB, Memory, Tools) for local vs production environments.
  - [ ] Create `proc-deploying-langgraph-agent-from-local-to-rhoai.adoc` (PROCEDURE) Step-by-step tutorial covering: (1) cloning and running the agentic-starter-kits LangGraph agent locally with Ollama/Llama Stack, (2) modifying provider configuration for RHOAI target environment, (3) deploying to OpenShift using the shared Helm chart (charts/agent/), (4) verifying the deployed agent REST API endpoint. Reference the upstream repo at github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits.
  - [ ] Create `proc-configuring-langgraph-agent-local-development.adoc` (PROCEDURE) Prerequisite procedure for local development setup: installing UV package manager, cloning the agentic-starter-kits repo, configuring run_llama_server.yaml for local Llama Stack server with Ollama, and running one of the LangGraph agent variants (react_agent, agentic_rag, or react_with_database_memory).
  - [ ] Create `ref-langgraph-agent-provider-configuration.adoc` (REFERENCE) Reference table documenting the provider configuration parameters for each capability layer (inference, vector storage, memory/state, tools). Show local development values vs RHOAI production values. Include the Helm chart values that control the provider swap (environment variables like LLAMA_STACK_BASE_URL, model server URLs).
  - [ ] Update `working_with_llama_stack/index.adoc` (ASSEMBLY) Add the LangGraph agent deployment tutorial to the existing RHOAI 3.4 Working with Llama Stack guide, likely as a new chapter or section under application examples. Link from the existing Llama Stack server deployment chapter.
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - [ ] Users can clone the agentic-starter-kits repository and run a LangGraph agent locally by following the local development procedure
  - [ ] Users can identify which provider configuration parameters to change when moving from local to RHOAI by consulting the provider mapping reference table
  - [ ] Users can deploy their locally-tested LangGraph agent to OpenShift using the documented Helm chart procedure without modifying agent application code
  - [ ] Users can verify the deployed agent is running by accessing its REST API endpoint as described in the verification steps
  - [ ] The tutorial documents all prerequisites including OpenShift version (4.19+), RHOAI version (3.4), Llama Stack operator activation, Python 3.12, and UV package manager
  - [ ] The concept module explains why the Llama Stack API enables code-free provider swapping and lists all four capability layers (inference, vector storage, memory, tools) with their local and production providers
  - [ ] The provider configuration reference includes the specific environment variables and Helm values needed for each provider swap
- **References**:
  - [RHAISTRAT-1393 Description](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393): Full feature description with provider mapping table, K8s artifact list, and acceptance criteria
  - [RHAIRFE-1172 Description](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172): RFE with clean acceptance criteria: config-only deployment, persistent state, consistent observability, REST endpoint
  - [RHAIRFE-1172 Comment (Participant C)](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172): Emphasizes MLflow tracing in inner loop is important for agentic evaluation — split to RHAISTRAT-1364
  - [RHAIRFE-1172 Comment (Participant D)](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172): WIP at github.com/MRGuziX/Agentic-Starter-Kits, pending work on vLLM via KServe (was using Ollama)
  - [RHAIRFE-1172 Comment (Participant F)](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172): AC points 1 and 2 completed (repo + readme), point 3 (MLflow) still missing
  - [RHAISTRAT-1049 Description](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1049): Parent outcome: Zero to Production developer journey, Phase 1 MVP content foundation, Phase 2 productization
  - [agentic-starter-kits repo](https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits): Production repo with LangGraph agents (react_agent, agentic_rag, react_with_database_memory, human_in_the_loop), shared Helm chart, and local/OpenShift deployment docs
  - [opendatahub-io agents examples](https://github.com/opendatahub-io/agents/tree/main/examples/langchain-langgraph): Upstream example referenced in RHAISTRAT-1393 as source agent pattern
  - [RHOAI 3.4 Llama Stack - Deploying server](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_ai_self-managed/3.4/html/working_with_llama_stack/deploying-llama-stack-server_rag): Existing docs for deploying Llama Stack server on RHOAI 3.4 — prerequisite for agent deployment

### High

#### REQ-002: Provider configuration swap reference (local vs RHOAI)
- **Source**: [RHAISTRAT-1393](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393) | [RHAIRFE-1172](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172)
- **Summary**: Both RHAISTRAT-1393 and RHAIRFE-1172 define a provider mapping table showing how each agent capability (inference, vector storage, memory/state, tools) maps from a local development provider to a production RHOAI provider. This requirement calls for a standalone reference document that enumerates every provider swap pair, the Llama Stack run.yaml configuration fields that control each swap, the LlamaStackDistribution CR equivalents for Kubernetes, and the environment variables involved. The reference is the linchpin that makes the 'no code changes' promise concrete and verifiable.
- **User impact**: Without this reference, developers must reverse-engineer which Llama Stack provider_type values to use for each capability when moving from local to production, and which run.yaml sections to modify. The reference table eliminates trial-and-error configuration and serves as the authoritative mapping between local convenience providers (Ollama, Faiss/Milvus Lite, local filesystem, local functions) and their enterprise-grade RHOAI counterparts (vLLM/llm-d via KServe, Milvus/PGVector via Llama Stack operator, PostgreSQL/Redis persistent storage, MCP tool servers).
- **Documentation action**:
  - [ ] Create `ref-llama-stack-provider-mapping.adoc` (REFERENCE) Provider mapping reference table with five capability rows (Orchestration, Inference, Vector DB, Memory/State, Tools) each showing: capability name, local provider_type, production provider_type, run.yaml config keys, LlamaStackDistribution CR fields, and notes on prerequisites.
  - [ ] Create `ref-llama-stack-run-yaml-parameters.adoc` (REFERENCE) Parameter reference for the run.yaml file covering: version, image_name, apis list, providers block structure (provider_id, provider_type, config), persistence/kvstore settings, and registered model entries. Include annotated examples for both a local-dev distribution and a production RHOAI distribution.
  - [ ] Create `con-provider-swap-architecture.adoc` (CONCEPT) Concept module explaining the Llama Stack provider abstraction layer, why configuration-driven swaps work without code changes, and how the run.yaml / LlamaStackDistribution CR encapsulate environment differences. References the mapping table for specifics.
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - [ ] Users can look up the local development provider_type and its production RHOAI equivalent for each of the five capabilities (orchestration, inference, vector DB, memory, tools) in a single reference table.
  - [ ] Each row in the provider mapping table includes the Llama Stack run.yaml provider_type value, the config block keys, and any prerequisite RHOAI components (e.g., KServe InferenceService for vLLM).
  - [ ] The run.yaml parameter reference documents every top-level key (version, image_name, apis, providers, metadata) with type, default value, and description.
  - [ ] The concept module explains why no application code changes are needed when swapping providers, linking to the Llama Stack provider plugin architecture.
  - [ ] At least two annotated run.yaml examples are provided: one for local development (Ollama + Milvus Lite + local filesystem) and one for production RHOAI (vLLM + Milvus/PGVector + PostgreSQL + MCP).
  - [ ] The LlamaStackDistribution custom resource fields that correspond to run.yaml provider sections are cross-referenced in the mapping table.
  - [ ] Environment variables that influence provider selection (e.g., LLAMA_STACK_BASE_URL) are documented with their purpose and default values.
- **References**:
  - [RHAISTRAT-1393 provider table](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393): Contains the five-row Component table (Orchestration, Inference, Vector DB, Memory, Tools) with Local Dev and Production columns.
  - [RHAIRFE-1172 capability table](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172): Contains the four-row Capability table (Inference, Vector Storage, State/Memory, Tools) with Local Development and Production (RHOAI) columns.
  - [RHAIRFE-1172 AC-1](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172): Acceptance criterion: 'A developer can deploy a locally-built LangChain/LangGraph agent to RHOAI by modifying only provider configuration, without changing application code.'
  - [RHAISTRAT-1393 AC-2](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393): Acceptance criterion: 'Documentation: A README explaining the local vs. remote configuration structure within the Llama Stack SDK.'
  - [agentic-starter-kits run_llama_server.yaml](https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits/blob/main/run_llama_server.yaml): Reference local-dev Llama Stack configuration using remote::ollama for inference, inline::milvus for vector_io, and PostgreSQL for persistence.
  - [agentic-starter-kits repository](https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits): Contains LangGraph agents (react_agent, agentic_rag, react_with_database_memory) and Helm charts for OpenShift deployment showing the local-to-production configuration patterns.
  - [OpenDataHub Llama Stack docs](https://opendatahub.io/docs/working-with-llama-stack/): Documents run.yaml structure, provider types per API (inference, vector_io, safety, tool_runtime), and LlamaStackDistribution CR for Kubernetes.

#### REQ-003: Kubernetes deployment manifests for LangGraph agents
- **Source**: [RHAISTRAT-1393](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393)
- **Summary**: Red Hat OpenShift AI 3.4 introduces support for deploying LangGraph-based agentic applications from local development environments to production OpenShift clusters. This requirement covers the Kubernetes manifests needed for that production deployment: a KServe InferenceService for vLLM model serving, a LlamaStackDistribution custom resource for unified provider configuration, a Deployment wrapping the LangGraph application (FastAPI/LangServe container with LLAMA_STACK_BASE_URL environment variable), a PersistentVolumeClaim for Milvus embeddings and agent checkpoints, and Service/Route resources to expose the agent REST API. Together, these artifacts allow users to deploy the same LangGraph agent that runs locally into an enterprise-grade OpenShift environment without code changes, relying solely on provider configuration swaps through the Llama Stack API layer.
- **User impact**: Users who have developed LangGraph agents locally need a documented, copy-paste-ready set of Kubernetes manifests and step-by-step instructions to deploy those agents onto OpenShift AI. Without this documentation, users must reverse-engineer each manifest from scattered upstream examples, leading to misconfigured deployments, missing PVCs, broken routes, or incorrect InferenceService settings.
- **Documentation action**:
  - [ ] Create `proc-deploying-langgraph-agent-to-openshift.adoc` (PROCEDURE) End-to-end procedure: prerequisites, creating each manifest, applying them in order, verifying the deployment. Should reference the provider swap concept and link to the LlamaStackDistribution reference.
  - [ ] Create `ref-langgraph-agent-kubernetes-manifests.adoc` (REFERENCE) Reference table listing each manifest artifact (InferenceService, LlamaStackDistribution CR, Deployment, PVC, Service, Route), its purpose, required fields, and annotated YAML examples.
  - [ ] Create `con-langgraph-agent-deployment-architecture.adoc` (CONCEPT) Architecture overview explaining how the six Kubernetes artifacts relate to each other: InferenceService serves the model, LlamaStackDistribution routes API calls, Deployment runs the agent container, PVC stores embeddings/checkpoints, Service/Route expose the API. Include a component diagram.
  - [ ] Update `proc-deploying-llama-stack-server.adoc` (PROCEDURE) Cross-reference the new LangGraph deployment procedure from the existing Llama Stack server deployment procedure, noting that LangGraph agents consume the Llama Stack server as a backend.
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - [ ] Users can create a KServe InferenceService manifest for vLLM model serving by following documented YAML examples with field-level explanations
  - [ ] Users can create a LlamaStackDistribution CR that configures the Llama Stack server to point to their cluster's vLLM, Milvus, and MCP tool instances
  - [ ] Users can create a Deployment manifest for their LangGraph agent container image (FastAPI/LangServe wrapper) with the correct LLAMA_STACK_BASE_URL environment variable pointing to the cluster Llama Stack service
  - [ ] Users can create a PersistentVolumeClaim manifest sized appropriately for Milvus embeddings and agent checkpoint storage
  - [ ] Users can create Service and Route manifests that expose the agent REST API and LangGraph Studio-compatible endpoint externally
  - [ ] Users can apply all manifests in the documented order and verify a successful deployment using the provided verification steps (pod readiness checks, endpoint health probes)
  - [ ] The architecture diagram clearly shows the relationship between the six Kubernetes artifacts and data flow between components
  - [ ] Prerequisites section lists required cluster capabilities (GPU nodes, Llama Stack Operator activated, KServe/OpenShift Serverless installed, container image registry access)
- **References**:
  - [RHAISTRAT-1393 Section 3.2](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393): Defines the six required K8s artifact types: InferenceService, LlamaStackDistribution CR, Deployment, PVC, Service, Route

#### REQ-004: Agent state persistence in production
- **Source**: [RHAISTRAT-1393](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393) | [RHAIRFE-1172](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172)
- **Summary**: LangGraph agents developed locally use ephemeral in-memory or file-based state (MemorySaver, SQLite) that is lost on process restart. When deploying to Red Hat OpenShift AI, agent state and memory must transition to durable, production-grade persistent storage — PostgreSQL (via the Llama Stack memory API and the LlamaStackDistribution CR) or Redis (via LangGraph's RedisSaver checkpointer). This documentation requirement covers the configuration-driven swap from local ephemeral storage to persistent backends, the Llama Stack memory provider abstraction that makes this transparent to application code, and the PersistentVolumeClaim and database prerequisites needed on OpenShift.
- **User impact**: Without this documentation, developers deploying LangGraph agents to RHOAI will lose agent conversation history, RAG context, and checkpoint state on every pod restart or scaling event, resulting in broken multi-turn conversations and failed agentic workflows. Users need clear guidance on configuring persistent backends so their agents maintain state continuity in production without code changes.
- **Documentation action**:
  - [ ] Create `con-agent-state-persistence-overview.adoc` (CONCEPT) Explain the two-layer memory model (short-term checkpoints vs long-term memory), local-vs-production storage backends, and how the Llama Stack memory API abstracts the provider swap
  - [ ] Create `proc-configuring-persistent-state-for-langgraph-agents.adoc` (PROCEDURE) Step-by-step procedure for transitioning from local MemorySaver/SQLite to PostgreSQL or Redis checkpointers when deploying to RHOAI, including LlamaStackDistribution CR memory provider configuration
  - [ ] Create `ref-agent-state-storage-backends.adoc` (REFERENCE) Reference table comparing storage backends (in-memory, SQLite, PostgreSQL, Redis) with latency characteristics, durability guarantees, scaling properties, and recommended use cases
  - [ ] Create `proc-configuring-postgresql-for-agent-state.adoc` (PROCEDURE) Procedure for setting up PostgreSQL as the persistent backend for Llama Stack metadata and agent state, including prerequisites (PostgreSQL 14+, credentials, network access), environment variables (POSTGRES_HOST, POSTGRES_PORT), and PVC configuration
  - [ ] Update `proc-deploying-langgraph-agent-to-rhoai.adoc` (PROCEDURE) Add state persistence configuration section to the main deployment procedure, cross-referencing the detailed persistence procedures and ensuring the Deployment manifest includes LLAMA_STACK_BASE_URL and checkpointer configuration
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - [ ] Users can identify which local storage backend (MemorySaver, SQLite, file-based) their LangGraph agent uses and its production-equivalent persistent backend
  - [ ] Users can configure PostgreSQL as the persistent state backend for their LangGraph agent on RHOAI by following the documented procedure without modifying application code
  - [ ] Users can configure Redis as an alternative checkpointing backend for LangGraph agents by following the documented procedure
  - [ ] Users can verify that agent state persists across pod restarts by resuming a multi-turn conversation using the same thread_id after a pod restart
  - [ ] The Llama Stack memory API provider configuration for local vs production environments is documented with concrete YAML examples for the LlamaStackDistribution CR
  - [ ] Prerequisites for persistent storage (PostgreSQL 14+ instance, PVC, credentials, network access) are enumerated with verification steps
  - [ ] The reference table documents latency, durability, and scaling characteristics for each supported storage backend (in-memory, SQLite, PostgreSQL, Redis)
- **References**:
  - [RHAISTRAT-1393 Description](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393): State Persistence pain point: local agents use in-memory state that must map to Redis/PostgreSQL in production
  - [RHAIRFE-1172 AC-2](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172): Acceptance criterion: Agent state and memory persist across pod restarts in production environment
  - [RHAIRFE-1172 Comment (Participant F)](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAIRFE-1172): Confirmation that basic repo and README for state persistence (points 1 and 2) are completed in agentic-starter-kits repo
  - [RHAISTRAT-1393 Provider Table](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393): Memory row: Local file system / SQLite -> PV - postgres etc. (enabled via the llama-stack memory API)
  - [OpenDataHub LangChain-LangGraph examples](https://github.com/opendatahub-io/agents/tree/main/examples/langchain-langgraph): Reference implementation of agent with state management
  - [OpenDataHub Llama Stack RAG agentic demos](https://github.com/opendatahub-io/llama-stack-demos/tree/main/demos/rag_agentic/notebooks): RAG agentic notebooks showing Llama Stack integration patterns
  - [Agentic Starter Kits - LangGraph React Agent](https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits/tree/main/agents/base/langgraph_react_agent): Completed starter kit with state persistence implementation referenced in RHAIRFE-1172 comments

#### REQ-005: MLflow observability and tracing for LangGraph agents
- **Source**: [RHAISTRAT-1393](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393) | [RHAISTRAT-1364](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1364)
- **Summary**: MLflow tracing must be integrated into the agentic starter kit agent templates (LangGraph, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Responses) to capture the full lifecycle of agent execution — including LLM calls, tool invocations, reasoning steps, inputs/outputs, and token usage. The integration uses mlflow.langchain.autolog() for LangGraph agents and must work with both local MLflow servers (for development) and MLflow instances deployed on OpenShift clusters (for production). This enables developers to debug, evaluate, and audit agent behavior across both environments without code changes.
- **User impact**: Developers building LangGraph agents on RHOAI gain end-to-end observability into agent execution flows. They can inspect each decision step, tool call, and LLM interaction through MLflow traces — both during local development with a local MLflow server and in production on OpenShift-hosted MLflow — enabling faster debugging, performance evaluation, and compliance auditing.
- **Documentation action**:
  - [ ] Create `proc-enabling-mlflow-tracing-for-agents.adoc` (PROCEDURE) Step-by-step procedure for enabling MLflow tracing in LangGraph agent templates: installing dependencies (mlflow>=3, langgraph, langchain_core), adding mlflow.langchain.autolog() call, configuring MLflow tracking URI for local vs OpenShift-hosted server, verifying traces appear in the MLflow UI
  - [ ] Create `con-mlflow-agent-observability.adoc` (CONCEPT) Concept module explaining what MLflow tracing captures for agentic workloads: graph execution traces, LLM call spans, tool invocation spans, token usage and cost tracking, and how OpenTelemetry compatibility enables integration with existing observability stacks
  - [ ] Create `ref-mlflow-tracing-configuration.adoc` (REFERENCE) Reference table of mlflow.langchain.autolog() parameters relevant to agent tracing: disable, run_tracer_inline (for async/ainvoke scenarios), and environment variables for MLflow tracking URI, experiment name; includes per-framework coverage matrix (LangGraph, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Responses)
  - [ ] Update `proc-deploying-langgraph-agent-to-rhoai.adoc` (PROCEDURE) Add observability section to the main deployment tutorial referencing the MLflow tracing procedure; include MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI environment variable in the Deployment manifest example
  - [ ] Update `ref-kubernetes-deployment-manifests.adoc` (REFERENCE) Add MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI and MLFLOW_EXPERIMENT_NAME to the environment variables table in the agent Deployment manifest reference
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - [ ] Users can enable MLflow tracing for a LangGraph agent by following the procedure with no more than 3 configuration steps
  - [ ] Users can verify that agent execution traces (including LLM calls, tool invocations, and token usage) appear in the MLflow UI after running the agent locally
  - [ ] Users can configure the MLflow tracking URI to point to an OpenShift-hosted MLflow instance and verify traces are collected in production
  - [ ] The concept module explains what data MLflow captures for each component of an agent execution (graph nodes, LLM spans, tool spans, metadata)
  - [ ] The reference table lists all configurable parameters for mlflow.langchain.autolog() with descriptions and default values
  - [ ] The per-framework coverage matrix clearly indicates which agent templates (LangGraph, LlamaIndex, OpenAI Responses) support MLflow tracing and any framework-specific limitations
  - [ ] The deployment tutorial includes the MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI environment variable in the Kubernetes manifest examples
  - [ ] The async tracing guidance (run_tracer_inline parameter) is documented for users combining autolog with manual @mlflow.trace decorators in LangGraph nodes
- **References**:
  - [RHAISTRAT-1393 AC-3](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393): Acceptance criterion: Observability showcased + MLFlow tracking using mlflow.langchain module, split to RHAISTRAT-1364
  - [RHAISTRAT-1364 Description](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1364): Full scope: instrument LlamaIndex, LangGraph, OpenAI Responses agent templates with MLflow tracing; support local and OpenShift MLflow servers
  - [RHAISTRAT-1364 AC](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1364): Six acceptance criteria covering integration into all templates, execution flow capture, metadata logging, dual-environment support, backward compatibility, documentation update
  - [agentic-starter-kits repo](https://github.com/red-hat-data-services/agentic-starter-kits): Target repository for MLflow tracing integration; current agents do not include MLflow tracing (Langflow agent uses Langfuse v3 instead)
  - [mlflow.langchain API reference](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/python_api/mlflow.langchain.html): API docs for mlflow.langchain.autolog() used to enable tracing
  - [MLflow LangGraph tracing guide](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/tracing/integrations/listing/langgraph/): Official MLflow docs for LangGraph tracing integration
  - [MLflow LangChain autologging](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/flavors/langchain/autologging/): Autologging documentation including run_tracer_inline parameter for async support

#### REQ-007: MCP tool integration via Llama Stack tools API
- **Source**: [RHAISTRAT-1393](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393)
- **Summary**: Red Hat OpenShift AI 3.4 introduces MCP (Model Context Protocol) server integration through the Llama Stack tools API, enabling LangGraph agents to transition from local tool functions (Python callables invoked directly) to enterprise MCP servers registered with the Llama Stack instance. This provider swap is configuration-driven: local tools use stdio transport and direct invocation, while production tools are registered as MCP toolgroups via SSE endpoints in the LlamaStackDistribution configuration or at runtime through the toolgroups.register() API. The MCP catalog (developer preview in RHOAI 3.4) and the MCP gateway (technology preview) further streamline discovery, deployment, and governance of MCP servers on OpenShift clusters.
- **User impact**: Users building LangGraph agents locally with simple Python tool functions need to understand how to register and consume those same tool capabilities as enterprise MCP servers when deploying to RHOAI, without modifying agent orchestration code. They must learn the MCP server registration process (toolgroup_id, provider_id, mcp_endpoint), the transport differences (stdio locally vs SSE/HTTP in production), and how to leverage the RHOAI MCP catalog and gateway for managed tool discovery and security.
- **Documentation action**:
  - [ ] Create `con-mcp-tool-integration-overview.adoc` (CONCEPT) Concept module explaining what MCP is, how it standardizes tool access for AI agents, and why it replaces direct local function calls in production. Cover the architecture: agent -> Llama Stack tools API -> MCP server -> enterprise API/service. Explain the two MCP approaches (registered remote servers via SSE and local servers via stdio) and when to use each.
  - [ ] Create `proc-registering-mcp-servers-with-llama-stack.adoc` (PROCEDURE) Step-by-step procedure for registering MCP servers with a deployed Llama Stack instance. Cover three methods: (1) runtime registration via Python SDK toolgroups.register(), (2) runtime registration via REST API, (3) declarative registration in run.yaml or ConfigMap. Include the toolgroup_id naming convention (mcp:: prefix), provider_id (model-context-protocol), and mcp_endpoint URI format.
  - [ ] Create `proc-transitioning-local-tools-to-mcp-servers.adoc` (PROCEDURE) Procedure documenting how to transition a local Python tool function into an MCP server, then register it with Llama Stack in production. Cover creating an MCP server (using FastMCP or similar), exposing it via SSE transport, deploying it on OpenShift (as a Deployment with Service), and registering the toolgroup with the LlamaStackDistribution. Include the Supergateway bridge for stdio-to-SSE conversion.
  - [ ] Create `ref-llama-stack-tools-api-parameters.adoc` (REFERENCE) Reference table for the Llama Stack tools API parameters: toolgroups.register() parameters (toolgroup_id, provider_id, mcp_endpoint, args), agent config toolgroups array, ConfigMap mcpServers array fields (name, uri, description), and supported transport types (SSE, streamable HTTP). Include the Tool Runtime API endpoint (/v1/tool-runtime) at Developer Preview level.
  - [ ] Create `ref-mcp-catalog-available-servers.adoc` (REFERENCE) Reference table listing MCP servers available in the RHOAI 3.4 MCP catalog by tier (Red Hat, partner, community), with server name, description, and supported capabilities. Note developer preview status.
  - [ ] Create `proc-using-mcp-tools-in-langgraph-agents.adoc` (PROCEDURE) Procedure for configuring a LangGraph agent to use MCP tools on RHOAI. Cover both approaches: (1) using Llama Stack registered toolgroups via the agent API with toolgroups array, and (2) using langchain-mcp-adapters MultiServerMCPClient with HTTP transport pointing to MCP servers on the cluster. Include code examples for agent_config with MCP toolgroup references.
- **Acceptance criteria**:
  - [ ] Users can explain the difference between local tool functions and enterprise MCP servers after reading the concept module
  - [ ] Users can register an MCP server with a Llama Stack instance using the Python SDK, REST API, or ConfigMap following the procedure
  - [ ] Users can convert a local Python tool function into an MCP server and deploy it on OpenShift following the transition procedure
  - [ ] Users can reference the tools API parameter table to correctly configure toolgroup_id, provider_id, and mcp_endpoint values
  - [ ] Users can identify available MCP servers in the RHOAI 3.4 catalog and understand their tier classification
  - [ ] Users can configure a LangGraph agent to consume MCP tools through Llama Stack or langchain-mcp-adapters following the agent integration procedure
  - [ ] Documentation clearly states the support level: MCP catalog is developer preview, MCP gateway is technology preview, Tool Runtime API is developer preview
- **References**:
  - [RHAISTRAT-1393 provider swap table](https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RHAISTRAT-1393): Tools row: Local Functions -> Enterprise MCP Servers (through the llama-stack tools API)
